Silhouette & Length.name: Floor-Length Anarkali
Silhouette & Length.description: The most dramatic Anarkali silhouette, falling all the way to the floor with a heavily flared skirt panel gathered from the waist. Named after the legendary courtesan Anarkali, this style creates maximum sweep and movement while walking.
Silhouette & Length.materials: Georgette, silk, or velvet with heavy embroidery panels
Silhouette & Length.notes: Requires the most fabric of any Anarkali style; often paired with a matching dupatta and churidar.

Silhouette & Length.name: Calf-Length Anarkali
Silhouette & Length.occasion: Semi-formal, day functions, office festive wear
Silhouette & Length.description: Falls to mid-calf, offering the flare and silhouette of a classic Anarkali with easier movement and a more contemporary, wearable length.
Silhouette & Length.notes: A popular choice for daytime festive events like Eid or Diwali visits where floor-length movement isn't practical.

Silhouette & Length.name: Knee-Length Anarkali (Anarkali Kurti)
Silhouette & Length.occasion: Casual festive, office wear, college functions
Silhouette & Length.description: A shortened, everyday version of the Anarkali silhouette, worn as a kurti with leggings, palazzos, or churidars. Retains the flared gather at the waist but in a far more casual, low-maintenance form.
Silhouette & Length.notes: The most commercially popular Anarkali variant today due to comfort and versatility.

Silhouette & Length.name: Double-Layer (Umbrella) Anarkali
Silhouette & Length.description: Two layered panels — often in contrasting colours or fabrics — are stitched to create extreme flare resembling an open umbrella, giving dramatic volume when spinning or walking.
Silhouette & Length.notes: Favoured for sangeet and reception functions where movement on the dance floor matters.

Fabric & Craft Tradition.name: Chikankari Anarkali
Fabric & Craft Tradition.description: Delicate white-on-white or pastel shadow-work embroidery, hand-done using the traditional Lucknawi chikankari technique, covering the yoke and body in fine floral and paisley motifs.
Fabric & Craft Tradition.materials: Fine cotton or georgette, hand chikankari thread work
Fabric & Craft Tradition.notes: Prized for its lightness and breathability, making it a favoured choice for summer and Ramzan/Eid wear.

Fabric & Craft Tradition.name: Zardozi & Gota Patti Anarkali
Fabric & Craft Tradition.description: Heavy metallic zari, gold/silver thread, and gota patti appliqué work cover the bodice and hemline, giving a regal, Nizami-court-inspired richness typical of Hyderabadi Anarkalis.
Fabric & Craft Tradition.materials: Silk or velvet, zardozi and gota patti embroidery
Fabric & Craft Tradition.notes: Among the heaviest and most expensive Anarkali variants; commonly seen at Hyderabadi and Lucknowi weddings.

Fabric & Craft Tradition.name: Mirror-Work (Sheesha) Anarkali
Fabric & Craft Tradition.description: Small mirror discs are embroidered across the body and sleeves in geometric patterns, drawing on Kutch and Rajasthani mirror-work traditions for a sparkling, folk-inspired look.
Fabric & Craft Tradition.notes: Especially popular for Navratri and garba-adjacent festive functions.

Fabric & Craft Tradition.name: Banarasi Silk Anarkali
Fabric & Craft Tradition.description: Cut from Banarasi brocade fabric with its signature woven gold zari motifs, adapting the traditional saree textile into the flared Anarkali silhouette.
Fabric & Craft Tradition.materials: Banarasi silk brocade with woven zari
Fabric & Craft Tradition.notes: A newer fusion trend that repurposes classic saree weaving traditions into suit form.

Fabric & Craft Tradition.name: Printed / Block-Print Anarkali
Fabric & Craft Tradition.description: Hand block-printed or digitally printed floral and geometric patterns on cotton, offering a lightweight, breathable Anarkali suited to everyday and warm-weather wear.
Fabric & Craft Tradition.notes: The most affordable and widely available Anarkali category in retail and online markets.

Neckline & Sleeve Style.name: Boat Neck Anarkali
Neckline & Sleeve Style.description: A wide, horizontal boat-shaped neckline that sits along the collarbone, often paired with three-quarter or full sleeves and heavy embellishment concentrated on the yoke.
Neckline & Sleeve Style.notes: A popular choice for contemporary designer Anarkalis seen at receptions and cocktail functions.

Neckline & Sleeve Style.name: Angrakha-Style Anarkali
Neckline & Sleeve Style.description: Features an asymmetric, wrap-style front closure inspired by Mughal angrakha coats, tied at the side rather than a straight front opening, adding a layered, regal drape to the bodice.
Neckline & Sleeve Style.notes: Draws directly on Mughal court dress, making it one of the more historically rooted Anarkali variants.

Neckline & Sleeve Style.name: Sleeveless Anarkali
Neckline & Sleeve Style.description: A modern adaptation with no sleeves or thin straps, often layered with a separate embellished jacket or cape, giving a fusion-forward take on the traditional silhouette.
Neckline & Sleeve Style.notes: Common in contemporary designer lines aimed at younger, fusion-wear buyers.

Regional & Bridal Variants.name: Hyderabadi Nizami Anarkali
Regional & Bridal Variants.description: Deeply influenced by Nizami court dress, combining rich velvet or silk bases with dense zardozi, kamdani, and pearl work, often in jewel tones like maroon, emerald, and royal blue.
Regional & Bridal Variants.materials: Velvet or silk, zardozi, pearl and kamdani work
Regional & Bridal Variants.notes: Closely associated with Hyderabadi Muslim wedding trousseaus.

Regional & Bridal Variants.name: Lucknowi Anarkali
Regional & Bridal Variants.description: Defined by fine chikankari and delicate pastel palettes, reflecting the understated elegance associated with Awadhi (Lucknowi) courtly fashion rather than heavy embellishment.
Regional & Bridal Variants.materials: Cotton or georgette, chikankari, pastel dyes
Regional & Bridal Variants.notes: Known for restraint and craftsmanship over sheer volume of embellishment.

Regional & Bridal Variants.name: Punjabi Anarkali
Regional & Bridal Variants.description: Bright, saturated colours combined with phulkari-inspired embroidery or thread work, paired typically with a contrasting dupatta and statement jewellery.
Regional & Bridal Variants.materials: Silk or cotton, phulkari-style thread embroidery
Regional & Bridal Variants.notes: Reflects Punjab's love of bold colour combinations and festive thread embroidery.

Regional & Bridal Variants.name: Bridal Heavy Anarkali
Regional & Bridal Variants.description: The most elaborate bridal category, combining a floor-length flared silhouette with dense embroidery across the entire body, a heavily worked dupatta, and often a trailing train.
Regional & Bridal Variants.materials: Silk or velvet, dense zardozi, sequins, stone work
Regional & Bridal Variants.notes: Frequently chosen as an alternative to a lehenga for the wedding or reception function, especially in North Indian and Pakistani bridal traditions.
